blocks.x: Okay, it's going. You can give your name first, Mr. Compton, your full name.
Well, my name is Glover John Compton.
Where were you born?
In Harrodsburg, Kentucky.
Was that near Louisville?
Yes, just below Louisville.
Can you tell your exact birth date?
Yes. January the 6th. 1884. A long time ago, isn't it?

Yeah, how old does that make you now? 75. 75, oh yeah. You look good for your age. Yes, I'm glad of that. Wish I was good as I look. Can you tell us about when you first started in music? Did your parents play any musical instruments? How did you get into music?

My mother's friend. See, my mother and father separated when I was four years old, so she told me. She had a friend that was a leader of a band. Not an orchestra. A brass band. And he taught me how to play a trumpet. Was that in your hometown? Yes. Exactly. When I was about 12, 14, I started out. And then I just picked up the piano myself. And the notes that I learned for this trumpet, well, I found out myself that they were the same as the notes for piano. And I never had a lesson for piano or anything. Not until this day I've never had a lesson. I just picked that up myself and went through with it. Got to a place when I was about 16 or 17, could play anything I heard. Maybe I used the wrong thing, which I evidently did. But I didn't have no trouble. From an ear standpoint, it sounded all right.
What kind of music did you play? What type of music did you play when you were a boy?
Well, they called it ragtime and syncopation, ragtime.
Remember any of the earliest pieces you first played?
Yes. One of my first pieces I got a lot of pleasure out of and quite a hit was I Ain't Bothered Yet. I don't think you've ever heard.
No, I don't know.

Talking about a man having a good time. It's no mistake, I certainly have my... I eat my chicken and shoot my own dead crabs. And I've always got a keg of gourd and gin on tap. Sometimes I may feel like taking a smoke. If I'm feeling kind of drowsy, I may use some dough. And there's one thing certain about the smoke, I've never yet sniffed any coke. But I've got my money on it. And I'm loving my honey strong. I ain't got a thing in the pond, eating and sleeping all day long. I ain't got no rent to pay. I'm just wasting my life away. To you folks, I've got nothing to say but all sure. I ain't bothered yet. That was the lyrics out of me. And it was strictly ragtime. It was quite a big hit with that thing. And I moved to Lulee then.
Where did you play? What were the first jobs you had?
Well, the first jobs I had was Lulee's, Tom Cole's, Jimmy Boyd at Tenth and Walnut. And then I played around all the houses, the pleasure houses.
Did they just use a piano? They didn't have a band? No, just a piano. Just a piano?
Just a piano around all the pleasure houses. And then two piano players at the Cosmopolitan Club, Tony Jackson and myself in Louisville.
That's where you first met Tony?
Yes. And he was a big hit there because he could sing good, you know.
About what year was that? How old were you? Do you remember?
In 1904. In 1904. I met Tony. Was he writing pieces himself? Did he have his own pieces those days?

No, he didn't have them in those days. He didn't start them until later on in Chicago, around 11, 1911 and 12. He was playing at the Elite number two because I was playing at the Elite number one. And Tony wrote Pretty Baby. Nothing like you ever heard it though.
Different words. You sang some of those words one time. Yes.

There's a certain girl in my neighborhood that I certainly am crazy about. In a certain way she stole my heart one day. And it's hers without a doubt. Now the other day while on my way just for a quiet stroll, I met this girl with brain of oil. Speaking of her jelly roll. She looked at me inside and then she gently replied. I gently replied. You may talk about your jelly rolls but none of them compare with my baby. My pretty baby. She's a tall doggy. I would be brown eyes and curly hair. I call her baby. My pretty baby. Maybe not today but there'll come a time when you hear those church bells chime. Kings and queens may reign supreme but none of them outshine this pretty baby of mine. That was his first lyrics. And actually when he sold it, he got some professional lyric writers to write some real lyrics for him.
It's ordinary. What was Tony like when you first met him? Was he a good pianist or did he sing most of the time?

He was a very good pianist, yeah. He always was good. We had some good ones here then. Oscar Holden, Tony Jackson, Clarence Jones, Ed Harden. Ed played at the Peekin Theater, 2700 State. That's where my wife and Lottie Grady was starred. Nettie Lewis and Lottie Grady. Your wife's name was Lewis? Nettie Lewis then. She wasn't my wife then. No. No. And Lottie Grady now she's got a tavern in Idlewild, Michigan.
Was the Peekin Theater then? Yes. Did they have the theater?
Yes, nice theater.
Was there a nightclub there too at that time?
No. Just the theater. Just the theater. Lightclub opened later.
Can you tell the first New Orleans band you ever heard? Who were the first musicians from New Orleans aside from Tony Jackson that you heard?

Well, the first one was a real band. It was Freddie Keppert. He was a great trumpet player. And a few years later the band broke up, which they all would form and then break up short. Oh, sure. When they got out of whack.
Do you remember about when you first heard Freddie Keppert? What year? Could you remember?
Yes, I heard Freddie Keppert around 14.
1914? Around 14, yeah. Who else was in the band? Did you remember any of the other fellows?
Yeah. Johnny Cincere. Bill Johnson was on bass. Johnny Cincere was on guitar. Yeah. Yeah.
Remember the clarinet player or the trombone who they were?
Well, the clarinet player then was a fellow named Slocum.
Slocum?
Yes.
I thought George Bakke maybe came up with him.
No, Slocum was a, I think Slocum was a West Indian, some foreign.
Oh, yes.
God, boy.
Do you remember the trombone?
Yes. A kid over there who played, yeah, used to play with Freddie. That's before Kidd went to Los Angeles.
Yes.
Went to Los Angeles long, about the latter part of the teens, around 18, 17, 18.

Do you remember a group that came up here with Manuel Perez and Lorenzo Teo? Do you remember? No, I didn't remember that. Or another, Tig Chambers, I think, was up here pretty early. Do you remember a cornet player, Tig Chambers?
No, I didn't know him. No. First trumpet players was Freddie Chambers and Tommy Ladner.
Oh, yes.
Tommy Ladner had a combination.
About four or six pieces, around six pieces. You played with Tommy, of course. You made that record. Can you tell me the first time you ever heard Tommy and when you played with him?
Well, I met Tommy, I guess, must have been around 11 or 12. Around 11 or 12. Around the days of when Jack Johnson opened up. 41 West 31st Street.
What did he have, a club or saloon or something?
Yes, the Cafe de Champions.
Oh, yes.

41 West 31st Street. Ed Harden was the first piano player he had. And I was corresponding with a friend of mine that plays beyond in Louisville, named Taylor, Will Taylor. He's a New York guy. He ended up a good musician. He studied music in quite a good arranger around New York. That was before Benny Carter.
Oh, yeah.
Benny Carter was a great musician. Great musician. Great arranger.
When did you play with Tommy Ladner first? Do you remember?
Oh, that was around 11. Tommy used to bring it. Tommy didn't have any band. He'd come around there and play with us. I don't know. The band really wasn't one of those cafe bands.
Oh, yeah.
It wasn't mine. It wasn't mine. It wasn't anyone else.
It just said that. It belonged to the cafe.
The boys at the Elite, yes. The Elite band.
Where was the Elite number one? What street? 3030 State Street. 3030?
Yes. And the number two, where was that? 3445 State Street.
Is that building? Is that building?
No, it's all down. It's all down. It's all down. They've played all those things up there.
I think I took a picture a few years ago of the number two. I never did see the number one.
Yeah, number two was right front. Tina and John.
Is that where Tony played?
Yes, that's where Tony makes it a lot.
Did they have a band there too or just piano?

Just a cafe band. A combination of lines. Carnet, you'd see a Carnet tonight maybe with him. Or Trumon tomorrow night you'd go and see a band or something else. Because Tony was featured. He was a star. I played at Tony's funeral.
Oh, you did?
Yes. And Charlie Young sang. A fellow from St. Louis.
Yes, you want to get through there? I'll stop it. Okay, it's going again.
In 24, the colored political boss of the South Side, like Dawson, you've heard of Dawson there? Yes, Mr. Day. Like Dawson yesterday. His name was Dan Jackson. And stop him if you can.
That's all right. Don't worry about it. It just won't pick it up too much.

And he sent for me. He was at 34th and Michigan, his headquarters. On the southwest corner. And he sent for me. And I went down to see what he wanted. And he asked me, how would I like to play for the mayor? I said, I thought he was kidding at first. I said, how? And how? I said. So he signed me up to play for Big Bill Thompson.
Oh, yeah.

It was coming up a few days or maybe weeks later. And I had to meet all these politicians. And we got the train here in Chicago and went to Alton, Illinois, by train. And when we got to Alton, there was a boat there. And the name of the boat. And the name of the boat was Cape Girardeau. Named after Missouri town.
I know that town.

And we got on this boat. And we got on this boat at Alton. And the boat went west to the Mississippi. And we cruised up and down the Mississippi River ten days from Peoria, Illinois, to Keokuk Island. And all the big towns like Quincy, Illinois, and St. Louis, Keokuk. And we'd stop overnight. And the boys would go out in town. So at Quincy, they all got off and went through the town. And when they come back, all the politicians had chambers, room chambers, you know. They went to a hardware store and bought all that the man had. And they came back on the boat. They had them all, it wasn't in them, but dust, because they'd never been used. And they'd never been used. And they'd all washed out. And the bartender had to fill them all with beer.
That's pretty interesting. Yeah, that handle on the side, you know.

And they were all drinking beer. I had a drummer named Sonny Christian. I don't know if you ever knew him. No, I never knew him. He was from Baltimore. So the man said, where's your, where's your, where's your, pot? Glover. He called me Glover. And I said, well, Your Honor, I haven't got any. Didn't bring me any. He said, they didn't. And I said, no, they didn't, Your Honor. So he said, well, come in and get mine. And he was over on the rails of the boat. So I left the piano, one of them got to get his. And he said, tell the bartender to rent it out and fill it up. So I took it in the bar and rent it out and I had one. And he got one for Sonny and from one of the other politicians. Judge Crowe, here, of Chicago, was State's Attorney's hand. Bob Crowe, he was a big shot then. He wasn't a big shot yet. But he was a State's Attorney's hand. Davey Miller, the prize fight referee, he was in politics. He was on that boat. He was Hachimilla's brother. Hachimilla got killed in the Pekin one, I think.
I heard there was some killing down there at the Pekin once. Yeah, Hachimilla. I think Joe Oliver was playing there then, I believe somebody told me. Joe Oliver's band was working.
There were so many different bands who played upstairs. The Pekin band was famous. Do you remember? The Pekin?
I mean combination. Well, that's alright. If you want to get your voice on here, it's alright too. Simon Stewart, yeah.
Simon Stewart and me, there was no band. Simon played and I sang.
You sang in the restaurant.
Simon Stewart, yeah.
Was that upstairs, Mrs. Compton? Yes.
Almost the whole space of the theater.
Was that after the theater?
No, during the theater. I saw the theater, came upstairs.
Oh, I see. You had the club upstairs.
I worked on the stage and would go upstairs.

I saw that place after it was a police station. Yeah. The policemen took me around, showed me some room upstairs. They said it had been the club. But downstairs they had the Black Mariah there where the stage used to be. That old, that was 27th Street, wasn't it? Yeah, 27th Street.
Showed me that years ago. Gee, that was a great theater then.
Isn't that where Shelton Brooks wrote? Yeah, some of these days. I believe somebody told me that some of the most famous actors and dancers that Bill Robinson used to wear. Oh, yes.
All the great stars of the stage used to come there.
Charlie Gilpin played Emperor Jones. Oh, yes.
Is that Gilpin? Charlie Gilpin.
Charlie Gilpin. Yeah, we worked there. We were in the same stuff company. You were in the same company.

Just past his room there on the right, coming in. Gilpin. On the left going out. He lived with us. He lived there. He lived there. When he went to Milwaukee, we went up there on a visit with him when he played Emperor Jones up there.
Yeah, those were some great times.
There was Florence Mills as a room too. That's Florence's picture up there.
Oh, Florence Mills.

Full dressed in male attire. Oh, yes. With the tail up the top there. There's Aunt Jemima there, right there. Right there, the Esaq Wilson. Oh, yes. That bottom picture. She's playing Aunt Jemima now. You see it on television. Oh, yes. That's Esaq.
There were some great stars in those days.

Yeah, that postcard picture up there on the piano. Two fellas, you see them walking along there. Oh, yes. That's me with the Almarilla. That's in Zurich, Switzerland. Oh. We just crossed the bridge. And was just walking on me and Frank Goody, alto saxophone player, a good one too.
Must have been summertime. It doesn't look like snow.

Yeah, it was summer. We went there in May. We went there in May. It was in May and June. See, when you go there, the police examined your papers, your passport, and your visa. Then they interviewed, asked you how long does your contract last? He looks at the contract. We told him two months. So, he folds it up and puts it in his pocket. The police puts all of our papers in his pocket. And tells him, now you'll get these papers back in 58 days. Two days before your retirement time expired. And sure enough, we did. We didn't see him anymore until then. We worked at Esprinade in Zurich. When did you first go to Paris? 26, 1926. 1926.
Yeah.
Brick shop sent from it. Brick's in Rome now.
Oh, she's still living then over there.
Yes, she's in Rome now. And, uh...
Was she a singer and entertainer too?
Yes. Yes. She worked at Jack. Jack Donaldson was her first job in Chicago.
I remember Jolly Roll Martin had talked about her once.
Yeah, oh yeah, Jolly do her very well.
But I never did know what type of singer she was, or if she just ran a club, or what?

No, she was raked. Like Ragtime, the one, they hadn't given them all that style of music all those different names in those days. Yeah. Ragtime, Swing, and I don't know what they're going to name it next. Rock and Roll. And it all comes under the heading of Ragtime. Yeah, I think so too. Every one of those different styles. And the drum is responsible for the different names. Different beats, you know, and then the different tunes. You mentioned that you knew Sidney Bichet over in Paris too. Yeah, this particular night of this trouble, they were, they were, they were, they come to Brick Tops and Sidney Bichet, and Sidney Bichet, and they were, they were, they were, they were, they were sitting there about half high, you know, which you usually was every night. Yeah. And the drum is responsible for the different names. And the drum is responsible for the different names. Different beats, you know, and then the different tunes. You mentioned that you knew Sidney Bichet over in Paris too. Yes, yeah, very, very well. Yeah, this particular night of this trouble, they were, they were, they were, they were, they come to Brick Tops and Sid was sitting there about half high, you know, which he usually was every night.
Yeah.

And everybody was giving them a little donation, so they asked Sid, and he didn't have any change on him. He didn't have any. So Mike McKendrick spoke of them and said, you should have some, if you don't get a hold of some, they'll be begging around here for you. And Sidney didn't like it. They had a big argument, and Mike and the bunch went, left there and went off to a place called Costa Bar. That's where we met, and we met over there. Mike was all in there drinking, in this Costa Bar that particular morning. Sid had evidently gone, see we left Sidney in Brick Tops. Yeah. And Sid evidently had went and got a revolver, when someone got a revolver. Mike had one in his pocket, but didn't nobody know it. Well, you know what, you can't revolve with it. Yeah. In the past, who wants a revolver in the pocket? And anyway, Sidney must have passed, evidently passed Costa Bar, and looked in there for Mike. And they had seen him, cause when they come out, Sid was, it had been hiding just below this bar, in a doorway. When they saw Mike get started out. Mike stepped out on the sidewalk, when we was leaving the bar, we were going on down to the bed. And I stepped out right, I was right behind Mike.
Yeah.

And when I stepped out, that's when the shooting was shot. And I guess the first shot got me, missed Mike, cause he couldn't shoot. And I didn't know I was shot, I didn't feel anything. Hit your knee? Right through the leg, right above the knee. And I didn't feel anything, so I didn't, when I put that right foot, the right foot evidently was in the air when, it was stepping out when I got it. Cause when I put it down, it wouldn't support me. And I found myself hopping on my left leg, and I hopped across the street, braced myself against this automobile, and so I could hop back around, and go back from whence I came. And I hopped back to the constant bar, and then the police came, rest of them both.
Did Mike get there any of them? No. You were the only one that got hit then.
The only one, the only American. Yeah. An English lady named Dolores Gibbons was shot through the right shoulder, and the right lung.
Oh, it must have been serious. It was, it was.

And an old French lady up the street was shot in the neck, glazing blow on the head. No. No. They took me to the hospital, the American hospital out in Nui. And when the trial came up, there was no witnesses against them. My God said they.
Yeah.
Cause they weren't, I didn't go to court cause it wasn't shooting at me.
No.

They had promised in the meantime that they were going to, all the time that I lost, they'd see that I was reimbursed for it. Yeah. Which they didn't do. And I didn't go. So, and after there was no witness against them, yeah, there had been evidence that some good lawyer would have got them dismissed. Yeah. No. No. No prosecuting witness against them. And the judge gave them 15 months each for shooting in the streets of Paris. Yeah. And that's what they got. And they did a little over a year of it. I think something like 12 and a half months or maybe 13. Yeah. Not quite all of them. Time off a good behavior now. Oh yeah. And they never gave me one, five cents.
They'd probably been drinking a good deal. Oh they were. They were.

See they used to, I was a beer drink over there. Same as I am here. And the back of them, they drank that brandy. Cognacs. Yeah. And whiskey. They were just collecting for a second. Yeah. And whiskey. They were just collecting for a second. Yeah. And whiskey. They were just collecting for a second. Yeah.
Okay, it's going. I'll make a note. This is part two of the Glover Compton interview. You were just saying they were collecting for some charity.
Yes, and Sidney said he didn't have any change on that particular night.
When was that? About which year?
Oh, that's late. I never did know the year.
Yeah, 1928. And Sidney didn't have any change on him, and Mike made that remark. He said he should have some. He better get some. They'll be begging for you around here.
He didn't like that.
He didn't like the remark.
Was Sidney working with the band? Were they together in the same band?
No, no. Mike was with Eddie South.
Oh, yes.

Eddie South's band. Eddie South was over there. You know who Sidney was playing with? No, with him. He played mostly with the white band, with the white fellas. Some of the French? Yeah, the French, yeah.
The band.
He always had his own band. And didn't do much playing in the Mo Mart. That was the sporting part.
Yeah.
Oh, he's a great musician, though, man.
Oh, yes.
And regarded himself.
That's right, yeah. He was the most popular musician in France, they say, when he died. Yeah, he was back in those days. In those days, popular too, huh?
Yeah, because nobody could play like him.
Did he play his clarinet mostly or his saxophone, soprano?
Clarinet and sax. Both of them, yes. And nobody could play like him.
No, they never did.
I don't think anybody plays like him today. No. He was tough. That, what's that, Peace City's...
Well, Petit Fleur was his number lately.
And then that great Newell Institute now. Down, down. Little, little, little, little, little, little, little, little.
Oh, High Society. High Society.
Nobody could play that like Sid. Gee, they used to make the French. People was crazy about him playing there.
How long did you stay in Paris then? Did you make several trips there or just stay there all those years?
I made trips back, but my trips back was visits here. I just stayed in Paris 14 years and 9 months. You came back when the war started? Oh, yeah, they'd run everybody back.
Yeah.

The American Council. Said for every American throughout Europe, the different councils of the different countries, and they told you what port and the date to be there to catch your boat back to America. And we went to, caught my boat, Unamay Carlisle. She's a great pianist. Oh, yeah. American. And we went to, had to go to Ireland to pick up some Americans. Some Americans were assigned to the same boat that we were assigned to in France. They went to Cove, every other town.
Yes, I've heard of that.

Yeah, Cove, Ireland. And when the boat left Ireland with these Americans, Unamay Carlisle was left. So when the boat pulled out about 30 or 40 feet out in the water, well, they heard a lot of yelling and going on. And they looked back, and that was a wave. So this guy reversed and backed up there together. I told her, gee, you're popular. She was a good entertainer.
Yes.
Good pianist.
Good looking girl too, wasn't she?
Yes. But a great pianist. She was a musician she was. She didn't play like we did. Yes, I'm picking up, she would buy all that music and play it. Could play it.
Were many American jazz bands over in Paris those years you were there? Did they come over all the time?
Yeah, they used to come over the big bands. Like, well, just before I left there, Glenn Miller.
Oh, yeah.
But back in the olden days, Paul Whiteman. And this was this great dance band, you know. Now, Bob Begarden, that's not it.
Ellington, I guess, he was over there too, wasn't he?
No, Ellington wasn't there the whole time I was there. No. But I used to come back, when I come back, and...
Did you see Armstrong over there? Yes, he sent for me.

I was in bed when he was in his friendship over there. He was at Brick Tops. Gee, he was glad to see me, and I was glad to see him, because I used to play with him, you know, yeah. Over here? At Dreamland 35, or 40, or 8.
Who else was in that band, at the Dreamland here?
That was Ollie Piles' band. He was the best nightclub singer I ever heard.
Really?
Yeah. Never heard anybody that I thought could sing as good as...
He's dead now?
Yes. I never heard anybody sing as good as Ollie. That's the... You, babe?
Uh-huh.
If you ever had any nightclub boy singing, could beat Ollie singing? No.
I think he was...
He was Tops.
He was Tops. Yeah. Can you tell us about that band with Jimmy Noon, and Tommy Ladner in that band regularly at the Dreamland? That record you made, you know, had Jimmy Noon on it.

Yeah, well, Jimmy played that with us that night. But he wasn't regular at Dreamland. Jimmy preferred that combo of his own. And when I left Dreamland, I joined Jimmy's band. Where was that? That was at Edelweiss. That's where we played. That was where every, from all the other nightclubs that come, that was Edelweiss. They don't play all night.
Where was that?
4816 State. What state?
And 75% was white. 75% of the clients.
Who else was in the band? You and Jimmy Noon and...

Jimmy Noon and Minor. Minor Hall, the drummer. And Baby Hall. One would play a week or four or five nights. Yeah. And you wouldn't see him anymore than his brother. Brother. And then we had Baby Dot there quite a long time, too. Johnny used to bring his clan out, too. Johnny was with Joe Oliver. Oh yeah. And he used to bring his clan out because he and Jimmy were very good friends. And he used to love to come out there and play. Ollie Powers. He used to do almost all the singing then, until he lost Baby, the Hall brothers. And then he played drums himself.
He was a good drummer, too.
Yeah, he was a good drummer. But he wasn't a drummer. Mine or Baby or Johnny Tartner. Wasn't as good as then with those boys.
Did you do much singing in those days or just play piano? I did a lot. I always had a lot of novelty songs. I've got a gang now. Oh yes, I've heard you sing all those late years.
Butterfly Kiss. I've got a wife and she's terrible. I wish I had her now. And Balls. Banquets and Parties. That's a great song. But it sounds like it's suggested, but it isn't.

No, that's right. That's what you think. I was going to ask about the New Orleans fellas when they first came up here. The bands like say Oliver. You heard Oliver and all of those. Yes. Did they seem much different than the Chicago bands? Well, yes.
Yeah, they brought something with them.
What was different? Did they have a different beat or a different melody or what kind of?

Yeah, they brought drummers here that made us all take notice. They played rhythms and things. The whole bunch and you know, and joined them. That played beats we'd never heard. They'd never been heard up this way. And couldn't change you know. In the different times. And then they brought all those ballads. They come up here playing all ballads in ragtime, jazz time. They started all that up here too.
Yeah.
The Swanee River. All of those.
All that kind of stuff.
And jazz. Not jazz, but ragtime. Yeah.
Do you remember some of the pieces you first heard them play, the New Orleans bands that played when they first hit town?

Yes, Saints was one of the best. One of the first good ones. I see they're imitating it now. You hear it on the radio now occasionally. Saints, Swanee River, Melancholy Baby, all of those kind of tunes. We'd been playing them. We never played them in no ragtime. Not like they did.
Did you ever work at Royal Garden?
No. I used to sit in. The girl that Louie married, white fat.
Oh yes, Lil Harden, Armstrong.
She's right away at 44.
Yes, I'm trying to see her tomorrow.
I'll tell her how long I'm here.
I will, yes.

Yes, she played over that. Occasionally, maybe once a month or so, go over and rest them up, peace, a tune. Can I sit in? Yes, sure. But I tell you, we used to see every week Benny Goodman. Every week, asking Joe, could he sit in at 35th and Calumet. Right around the corner, yes.
Oh yes, the Sunset, was that, or the Plantation? Plantation, that was it.
He'd ask Joe, could he sit in? Yes. I called Joe, Mr. Toon. Mr. Joe, yes.
Mr. Holliday.
Can I sit in? Yes, he lived on the west side. He could play then. All right.
Benny Goodman could play then. Who was the best trumpet player from New Orleans you heard? Did you like Keppert or Oliver, Tommy Ladner? Who was your favorite? Oliver.
Oliver. Yeah, he's the best of them all, including Louie.
Really? Including Louie, yeah. Yeah.
Joe stood up. Louie had stayed seated in Joe's band. And the breaks, you know, the breaks out of that, every tune had a break in there for a trumpet, a couple of bars or something.
They made some records.

Joe did all of that. And then a lot of people after Louie had been here about a month or so, the people down in the audience used to say, let the kid, give the kid a break Joe. Give the kid a break Joe. Give the kid a break. And Joe started giving Louie those breaks. Louie was a high note trickster better than Joe I think, making him a high note.
Yeah, he does a lot of that to me.
But Joe was the best going through a whole entire tune. He was tight.
How did the Johnny Dodds and Jimmy Newton compare? Oh, Jimmy Newton.

Well, Johnny Dodds was the best clarinet player. That's where everybody claimed, everybody couldn't be wrong. But Jimmy had the best business head. See, Jimmy was always up front on paper on the contract. Yeah. Yeah, he was always out front on the front. Be the leader. Yeah. You knew what everybody in the band was getting, but you never knew what Jimmy was getting, because he always signed the contract.
Yeah.
And Johnny Dodds didn't. See, Johnny didn't go out for a combination.
He was sort of a quiet fellow. I knew both of them.
Yeah, Baby was more front man than Johnny. Yeah, that's right. Johnny's being quite a very good trumpet. Very good at the Atlantic playing.
Did you ever work at the Deluxe or Deluxe? Where was that? That's Jelly's play spot.

Oh, yeah. Jelly's play spot. See, we all had a spot. Yeah. He liked number two was Tony's spot. He liked number one was my spot. And Deluxe, Frank Pria and Bill Bottoms was there. Jelly Rolls Montage.
Was that on 35th Street?
3503 State.
Just south of 35th Street. I thought that was near Indiana. Was that Entertainer? No, I don't remember the place.
Entertainer's near Indiana. On the south side of the state. That's what I'm thinking of. Could no combination playing in the Entertainer's. You had to have a big band. That's a great big place.
Oh, it was. I never got inside.
Yeah, Freddie Kemper.
Did a lot of work in there. A lot of he and his bike. Can you tell me more about Jelly Roll when you first heard him about how early he got up here?

Well, I heard Jelly. Jelly and I were pretty close. We did a lot of running around together. Around, around, during the fair in Frisco. I come back here then. Jelly was raising a heck around here then. That was 1915 when I come back to Chicago from San Francisco after the fair. And then we went back to California and Jelly went back. Jelly waked at the Cadillac and we waked at the Waldorf.
In Los Angeles?
Los Angeles.
Where did you play in San Francisco? Was that Barbary Coast going then? Yes, yes.
I played at the St. Francis Club.
Oh, yeah.

My wife waked at it so different. Lou Purcell's place. Leicester Map. There was 43 saloons in two blocks. You never saw them there? On Pacific Street, huh? Yeah. Never saw them. Well, you got to take one of them.
No, but I've seen it in late years. There wasn't much there. But there was still a little bit there. When I went out in 1940 about, they still had part of it. I right out of one doing nothing.
I didn't do nothing. All the way up the seat on both sides.

Tell me, did the district here in Chicago use piano players much? Did you ever work any of the houses there? No, they worked at any houses in Chicago. We're working all of them in Louisville. In Louisville. Not up here. All the big houses. Did the big places like the Everly Club, were they running when you were here?
Yes.
Did they use a piano player?
Yes, but mostly all white.
Did Tony or Jelly ever play at these places? No, not at the Everly Club, no.
They used, uh, Nora Holt. Played at the Everly Club for years.
Babe, that's a doorbell. I don't want to keep you long, but we'll be through here in a few minutes. Did you play with me?
The bell right. The bell right. Oh, I can't go.
You want to go, or should I go? There. Okay, it's going again.

See, my entertainers in the past were all the old-time well-known American white entertainers. Roy, Roy was a, he and I alternated at the piano. Roy Barton. Roy Barton. Oh, yeah. Chicago boy, Irish boy. And Paul Farrell. And Bill Hanley. That was my entertainers at the Irish New York bar five years. And then at the Royal Box, so we could Cricket Smith. There are two bands out of the Royal Addison. Big plays where all the big stars like Mr. Bowler, Alderman of the Northside, Alderman of the 43rd of Watt, Patty Bowler, and the Mayor Cermak that got killed out there. Oh, yes. Yeah, they used to come to the Royal Box, all that, that class of people. High class people.
In the old days here in Chicago, were there many gang fights around when you were playing here in the Prohibition? No, no. Has Al Capone taken over yet or not? No, no. I never, never saw a fight.

They didn't do any fighting much around there. They just got to their man. If they'd get caught their man in one of those places, wouldn't be no much of a fight. Those fellas, you see, they didn't do much fighting. They just got the man. Yeah.
When he's mobbed, he's mobbed, he's mobbed.

Took them for a ride. The only way he could have any more success in life is to leave town. Yeah. High grossing moustaches and whiskers and something, disguise himself. Because they'd get you, you could not get away once you were mobbed. And then they didn't bother no strangers.
Did the gangsters control the dance halls? Who ran the E-Light in all those places?
Art Cardoza and Tina and Jones run the E-Light. Bill Bottoms run the Dreamlin. And Frank Preyer run the Deluxe, by the way I tell you.
Were most of those people colored? Colored, yes.
They were colored. They all colored.
So it wasn't any gangster control then. Oh no.
They were, we used to love to see the gangsters, so-called gangsters coming in, because they were the best tempers.
Yeah. But they didn't own the places that run them then.
No, they didn't run any of these places. The places they run was down around 22nd. Yeah. We used to go down there, down to Big Jim Colosimo.
Oh yeah, I've heard of that. Yeah. Yeah. But they didn't run the E-Light or Royal Garden or Dreamland and those places.

Now, I had a club here in 41 and just, you're walking, just like walking in an ordinary tavern. And my first table was blackjack. The next table was the walled-in and rubber-lined dice table. An old pool, it had been an old pool table and you had those sides put on it and lined with rubber. Oh yeah. And then a poker table. And I had to, or Big Jim Colosimo, I had to go down to see Colosimo. And I was okayed. I was okayed for those people.
Most of the customers, were they colored or white in those clubs along State Street?

More about, oh, I'd say 70 or 75 percent white. At the E-Light and Dreamland and those places. Yeah. We'd get the white crowds around 12 or 1 o'clock every night. See, the E-Light and Dreamland had balcony all the way around. And the whites, a lot of, every night we'd get a bunch of, about 20 or 30 or more white fellas with tuxedos on. So naturally we knew there were musicians coming from that yard around 1 or 1.30. Was there dancing at most of those places or mostly just drinking or what? Yeah. Dancing and drinking and they usually had a couple of entertainers. Girls. Nettie and Caroline and the James sisters. Nettie could name them better than I could.
Nettie and Caroline and the James sisters. Nettie and Caroline and the James sisters. Did you have any trouble with the Prohibition raids in those days? No, no, no, no.
Never started, never, never was in a raid the whole time I played in those places.
And that was after Prohibition too?
Yes. Did they sell? No, before Prohibition. Before Prohibition too? Yeah. Because I went to the E-Light 1910.

I was going to ask a little bit more about Tony Jackson and Jelly Roll. What style of piano they played? Did they play much different style ragtime than yours or was it about the same kind of ragtime?
About the same kind. Only Jelly was best without songs.
Just plain instrumental piano songs.

Yeah, yeah. Jelly was best without songs. Tony was best with songs. And then this other boy came here, Harry Collins, came here around twenty. Around nineteen, now twenty. And he brought a young fella here from Pittsburgh. And he introduced, brought him to me because I was one of the best known of the fellas. And told me to look after him. And I said I would. So I carried him around and introduced him all over the other side. Who was that, Earl Hines?
Earl Hines, yeah.
And then I was playing for all the prize fights then.
That's all, you won't bother you.

There had a few fights. One over the entertainers and one, Jack Nelson had one at 47th Street. And I used to take Earl with me and we had up on a stand ready to go up a ladder. And then I'd put Earl up there and I'd come on down sitting with the gang, the hustlers, the pimps and things. And then we'd all sit down and listen to Earl. So they used to say, who is that kid you got up by Glovin? And I said that's a boy from Pittsburgh called Earl Hines. He said, you can play, can't he? I said, you telling me? He was good then.
Oh, he was good.
He was good. And then when I left, went to Europe in 26 wide, Earl took my job with Jimmy Newman at the Apex. The Apex. Yeah. Earl took over. That was my job. If I had stayed in.
You hadn't started at the Apex, so you'd been up on 40. No.
They were building it, yeah. On State Street. Uh-huh. They were building the Apex, yeah. That's why Walter Burton got killed up there too.
Oh, yeah. Were these New Orleans bands more popular than the Chicago bands? Yes. Do you think the people liked them better?

Yes. They could play, they could play better. No mistake about it, they could play better. There wasn't no Chicago band to equal Joe Otto's band. Nothing to even approach it. Now the musicians, why are you going to get a trombone player to play like Kid Ora?
No.

No. I don't know. You see, the boys wasn't here. We had a lot of clanded players, and the fellas around here played all of them, and they're not as good as those boys. The trumpet players were not as good as Freddie Kepp or Tommy Ladner, or Lou Armstrong or Joe Otto. We didn't have any trumpet players that good. There was a lot of them around here boys could play. They could play for music or for air, but not like Joe and those boys. And the most playing that those boys did was for air, it wasn't for music. Most playing. Because a musician that's been educated, that's been studying music a long time, just don't have that in his head, I don't know what it is, that the air player's got. They don't have it. They don't have it. They don't have it. You see a father can read, and then play, hear something and play it. They're the best. That is playing. Swing or jazz, the right time. I believe once your wife told me that she worked with P.G. Laurel, did she travel with him? Yeah. Babe? Yeah. Yeah.
Give me a minute. Did you travel with, was it a show, was it P.G.? Four Pawn and South Brothers Circus, and he had the band in the sideshow.
And did you play in the band?
No. Or sing? He taught me cornet, but I didn't know. I didn't know. I didn't know.
I didn't know. I didn't know. I didn't know. I didn't know. I didn't know.
I didn't know. I didn't know. I didn't know. Or sing.
He taught me cornet, but I didn't play with the band.
Oh, you didn't play with it?
No, but you see in the sideshow they had a female quartet and a male quartet. Oh, yes.
And the band.
And I was with the female quartet.
That was P.G. Lowry. P.G.
Lowry. L-O-W-R-Y.
L-O-R-Y. L-O-R-Y.
I had that. D-O-W-R-Y. D-O-W-R-Y. D-O-W-R-Y. D-O-W-R-Y. D-O-W-R-Y. D-O-W-R-Y. D-O-W-R-Y. D-O-W-R-Y. D-O-W-R-Y. D-O-W-R-Y. D-O-W-R-Y.

segments.title: Opening: name, birthplace and birth date
segments.summary: Compton gives his name, Harrodsburg, Kentucky birthplace and January 6, 1884 birth date.

segments.title: Learning trumpet, teaching himself piano, first ragtime pieces
segments.summary: A bandleader friend of his mother taught him trumpet; he taught himself piano by ear and played ragtime, including the hit 'I Ain't Bothered Yet'.

segments.title: First jobs in Louisville pleasure houses and meeting Tony Jackson
segments.summary: Solo piano in Louisville houses and clubs; he and Tony Jackson were the two pianists at the Cosmopolitan Club in 1904.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists and New Orleans bands
segments.title: Tony Jackson, Pretty Baby, and Chicago pianists and the Pekin Theater
segments.summary: Jackson wrote Pretty Baby in Chicago around 1911-12; Compton names other pianists and the Pekin Theater where his wife starred.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists and New Orleans bands
segments.title: First New Orleans band heard: Freddie Keppard's group
segments.summary: Keppard's band c. 1914, with Bill Johnson, a guitarist, a clarinetist named Slocum and a trombonist who later went to Los Angeles.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists and New Orleans bands
segments.title: Tommy Ladner, Cafe de Champions and the Elite band
segments.summary: Other early trumpeters, and how he met and played with Tommy Ladner at Jack Johnson's Cafe de Champions around 1911-12.

segments.chapter: Chicago pianists and New Orleans bands
segments.title: The Elite clubs on State Street and Tony Jackson's funeral
segments.summary: Addresses of Elite No. 1 and No. 2, the cafe bands there, and Tony Jackson as the featured star.

segments.title: Mayor's riverboat cruise, 1924, and politicians aboard
segments.summary: Politician Dan Jackson hired Compton to play for Mayor Big Bill Thompson on a ten-day Mississippi riverboat trip. Judge Crowe and Davey Miller were aboard; talk turns to a killing at the Pekin and its famous band.

segments.title: Nettie Compton on the Pekin theater, club upstairs and stage stars
segments.summary: Nettie and Simon Stewart performed upstairs; stars like Charles Gilpin and Florence Mills passed through the theater.

segments.title: Photo from Zurich: touring Switzerland with a band
segments.summary: Compton describes a photo in Zurich and how the police held their papers during a two-month contract.

segments.title: Going to Paris in 1926 and Bricktop
segments.summary: He first went to Paris in 1926; Bricktop, who began in Chicago, sent for him.

segments.title: Ragtime as the umbrella for all later styles
segments.summary: He says ragtime, swing and rock and roll are all one music, and the drums give the different names.

segments.title: The shooting in Paris: Sidney Bechet and Mike McKendrick
segments.summary: Compton's account of a quarrel at Bricktop's and the shooting outside the Costa Bar in which he was hit above the knee.

segments.title: Aftermath: trial, sentences and the remark that provoked Bechet
segments.summary: No witnesses appeared, the shooters got about a year, he was not reimbursed; the dispute began over a charity collection in 1928.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet's playing and standing in France
segments.summary: Mike McKendrick was with Eddie South; Bechet led his own band, played clarinet and sax, and was beloved in France.

segments.title: Leaving Paris at the war's start and pianist Una Mae Carlisle
segments.summary: He stayed in Paris 14 years and 9 months, was sent home by the American consul, and sailed with Una Mae Carlisle.

segments.title: American bands in Paris and seeing Armstrong at Bricktop's
segments.summary: Whiteman, Glenn Miller and others visited; Armstrong was glad to see him, having played with him in Chicago.

segments.title: Ollie Powers and the Dreamland band
segments.summary: The Dreamland band was Ollie Powers's, with Armstrong; Compton calls Powers the best nightclub singer he ever heard.

segments.title: The Edelweiss band with Jimmie Noone and the Hall brothers
segments.summary: After Dreamland he joined Noone's band at the Edelweiss, with Minor and Tubby Hall, Ollie Powers and his own novelty songs.

segments.title: How the New Orleans bands differed from Chicago bands
segments.summary: New Orleans drummers brought new rhythms, and ballads played in ragtime; Saints and Swanee River.

segments.title: Sitting in at the Royal Garden; Lil Hardin and Benny Goodman
segments.summary: Compton sat in at the Royal Garden and saw Benny Goodman ask Jimmie Noone to sit in at the Plantation.

segments.title: Oliver versus Armstrong, and Johnny Dodds versus Jimmie Noone
segments.summary: He rates Oliver the best trumpeter, discusses Louis's breaks, and compares Dodds and Noone as players and businessmen.

segments.title: Everyone's spot: the Deluxe, Entertainers Club and Keppard
segments.summary: Jelly Roll, Tony and Compton each had a favorite spot; the Deluxe and Entertainers' Club on State Street.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton, San Francisco fair and Los Angeles
segments.summary: Compton ran around with Jelly Roll; played the St. Francis Club on the Barbary Coast and returned to Chicago in 1915.

segments.title: Piano players in Chicago houses and the Everleigh Club
segments.summary: He worked houses in Louisville, not Chicago; the Everleigh Club used mostly white players such as Nora Holt.

segments.title: The Royal Box and its high-society clientele
segments.summary: Between interruptions he lists his entertainers at the Irish New York bar and the Royal Box, frequented by aldermen and Mayor Cermak.

segments.title: Gangsters, Prohibition and who ran the State Street clubs
segments.summary: He says gangsters did not run the Black-owned clubs, which were run by Black proprietors; gangsters ran places around 22nd.

segments.title: His own gambling club and the mostly white crowds on State Street
segments.summary: Compton ran a club with gambling tables, cleared with Colosimo; the crowds were 70-75 percent white and there were no raids.

segments.chapter: Piano styles and New Orleans superiority
segments.title: Tony Jackson and Jelly Roll's styles; mentoring Earl Hines
segments.summary: Jelly was best without songs, Tony with songs; Compton introduced Earl Hines around town, and Hines took his Apex job in 1926.

segments.chapter: Piano styles and New Orleans superiority
segments.title: Why New Orleans bands outplayed Chicago's
segments.summary: He argues that the New Orleans players, especially Oliver, Keppard, Ladner and Armstrong, played better, by ear rather than by training.

segments.title: Nettie Compton's circus work with P.G. Lowry
segments.summary: Nettie sang in a female quartet in a circus sideshow; the transcript degrades into repeated spelling of Lowry.
